title: Pricing arranging work and being asked to work for exposure
summary: Setting a fee is hard; a record company told him he should be happy to be on a Woody Herman record.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Did you have a way of determining a price for your work and how did it change over the years?

That’s a rough one. That is hard. Because you never know what to charge. You know the worst thing you can hear a producer say is, “Thank you for being so reasonable.” That’s the last thing you want to hear. You know what? You get a sense of what the bandleader or the client can pay. You get a sense, and you hit them with a figure. And you just hope they will come back with something, or they don’t say get lost. It’s hard. Because you know every market is different. Like for Buddy Rich a lot of people don’t know this but I rarely got paid by Buddy. A lot of stuff I had to scream and yell trying to get paid. He didn’t have the money. He was used to, as a star, having anything he wanted. He just would spend — I’ll buy this — and a lot of times the manager didn’t have the money to pay me. And when I had friends that were managers, like Stanley Kay, he would go to bat for me, he’d find the money somewhere. He’d maybe take an extra couple of hundred here. But having said that, Buddy gave me all of the publishing rights to everything I had done for him. He knew, he knew that was a valuable thing. Woody Herman didn’t. Maynard Ferguson didn’t. Count Basie didn’t. They would grab the publishing, as rightfully they should. Buddy gave me a hundred percent of everything. So that was the payback. It was rough at the time but you know, the payback is there.
Did you ever have a manager or bandleader say, “Come on, John, this would be good exposure for you”?

Yeah. I had that happen. I had a record company out in California, one of Woody’s recordings. The guy said, “Well we don’t pay that kind of money for arrangements” and you know, “this is something you should be happy, you’re going to get your stuff on a Woody Herman record.” Yeah. I’ve got stories. There’s a lot of stories out there.
